<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXIII.—Emperor Ri-chiū (Part III.—His Rebellious Brother and the Latter’s Retainer Sobakari are Slain).}}]}}

Thereupon his younger brother His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake came, and sent [to ask for] an audience.<ref>The original of this clause is very elliptical, consisting only of the two characters {{Japanese|令謁}}. The old reading joins thereto the characters {{Japanese|爾天皇}}, which according to Motowori form the commencement of the next sentence. The meaning is not affected by the change.</ref> Then the Heavenly Sovereign caused him to be told [these words]: “As I am in doubt whether perhaps Thine Augustness may [not] be of like mind<ref name=p289>Literally, “heart.” Similarly below, where the word “intent” is used in the translation.</ref> with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, I will not meet and speak with thee.” [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] replied, saying: “I have no evil intent. I am not of like mind with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu.” [The Heavenly Sovereign] again caused him to be told [these words]: “If that be so, [do thou] now return down, and slay King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, and come up [again hither]. At that time I will surely meet and speak with thee.” So he forthwith returned down to Naniha, and deceived [a man] named Sobakari,<ref>The signification of this name is quite obscure.</ref> a man-at-arms<ref>''Hayabito''. The reader should compare {{nsl2|Sect. XXXVIII, Note 11|../Section 38#cite_note-11}}.</ref> in the personal service of<ref>Literally, “closely accustomed to.”</ref> King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, saying: “If thou wilt obey my words, I shall become Heavenly Sovereign, and will make thee prime Minister, to rule the Empire.<ref>The original leaves it uncertain whether the words “to rule the Empire” should be applied to the speaker, to Sobakari, or to both; and the ambiguous application has therefore been preserved in the translation.</ref> How [would this be]?” Sobakari replied, saying: “[I will do] according to thy {{hws|com|command}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/376 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|290|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXVIII.}}}}</noinclude>{{hwe|mand|command}}.” Then plenteously endowing that man-at-arms, he said: “If that be so, slay the King.” Thereupon Sobakari watched for the time when his King went into the privy, and thrust him to death with a spear. So when [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] was making his progress to Yamato taking Sobakari with him, he, on reaching the entrance of the Ohosaka mountain, thought [thus]: “Although Sobakari deserves very well of me, he has truly<ref>Literally, “already.”</ref> slain his lord. This is unrighteous. Nevertheless if I reward not his deed, I may be called untruthful; and if I quite carry out my promise, his intentions are on the contrary to be feared. So, though recompensing his deed, I will destroy his actual person.” Therefore he said to Sobakari: “I will halt here to-day and bestow on thee the rank of Prime Minister, and to-morrow will [continue my] progress up.” So a halt was made at the entrance to the mountain, a temporary palace forthwith built, a copious feast<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CVII, Note 7|../Section 107#cite_note-7}}.</ref> suddenly held, the rank of Prime Minister forthwith bestowed on the man-at-arms, and all the officials<ref>Literally, “the hundred officials,” a Chinese phrase, which has been met with before.</ref> made to do obeisance [to him]. The man-at-arms, delighted, thought that he had accomplished his design. Then [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] said to the man-at-arms: “To-day I will drink liquor from the same cup as the Prime Minister.” And when they drank together, a bowl<ref>The character {{Japanese|鋺}} used in the text implies by its radical that the bowl was of metal. It is an unauthorized form of {{Japanese|椀}} or {{Japanese|盌}}.</ref> large [enough] to hide the face was filled with the liquor presented.<ref>''Scil.'' by the prince to the man-at-arms.</ref> Hereupon the King’s child drank first, and the man-at-arms drank afterwards. So when the man-at-arms was drinking, the great cup covered his face. Then [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] drew forth a sabre which he had laid under the matting, and cut off the head of the man-at-arms. Forthwith on the morrow he made his progress up. So the place was called by the name of Chika-tsu-Asuka.<ref name=p290>''I.e.'', Nearer Asuka. The name is written {{Japanese|近飛鳥}}. The student should consult Motowori’s note on this passage in Vol. XXXVIII, pp. 38–39 of his</ref> Going up and reaching Yamato,<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/377 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXVIII.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXXXIV.}}|291}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><ref follow=p290>Commentary, to see what can be done towards reconciling the name, the characters it is written with, and the origin ascribed to it, all of which are so apparently incongruous.</ref>he said: “I will halt here to-day and, having purified myself, will go forth to-morrow and worship at the temple of the Deity.”<ref>''Scil.'' of ''Isonokami''. This deity was the sword forming the subject of the legend narrated in {{nsl2|Sect. XLV|../Section 45}}.</ref> So that place is called by the name of Toho-tsu-Asuka.<ref>{{Japanese|遠飛鳥}}, i.e. Further Asuka. ''Conf.'' {{nsl2|Note 11|#cite_note-p290-12}}.</ref> So going forth to the temple of the Deity of Iso-no-kami, he sent to report to the Heavenly Sovereign that he had come up to serve him after accomplishing the work [with which he had been entrusted].<ref>This is the gist of the original phrase, which will not bear literal translation into English: {{Japanese|政既平訖参上侍之}}.</ref> So [the Heavenly Sovereign] sent for, and met, and spoke with him.
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXIV.—Emperor Ri-chiū (Part IV.—Various Deeds).}}]}}

The Heavenly Sovereign thereupon first appointed the Suzerain of Achi to the office of Treasurer,<ref>In Japanese the same word is used for a “store-house” and for the “treasury.” But the appointment here mentioned would seem really to correspond to what we should call Lord of the Treasury or Minister of Finance. The characters in the original are {{Japanese|藏官}}.</ref> and likewise bestowed on him domains.<ref>Literally, “ration grounds.”</ref> Again in this august reign the name of Waka-sakura Tribe<ref>''Waka-sakura-be''.</ref> was granted to the Grandees of the Waka-sakura Tribe.<ref>''Waka-sakura-be no omi''. Conf. {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXI, Note 1|../Section 131#cite_note-1}}.</ref> Again the gentile name<ref>All the editors agree in here reading as ''kabane'' (“gentile name,” see {{nsl2|Sect. XIV, Note 5|../Section 14#cite_note-5}}) the character {{Japanese|姓}}, which signifies properly “family name.”</ref> of Dukes of Himeda<ref>''Himeda no kimi''. Nothing is known of this family.</ref> was granted to the Dukes of Himeda. Again the Ihare Clan<ref>''Ihare-be''. For Ihare see {{nsl2|Sect. XLIII, Note 6|../Section 43#cite_note-6}}. It will be remembered that the Emperor of whose reign the present Section forms part held his court at Ihare.</ref> was established.<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/378 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|292|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXVIII.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXV.—Emperor Ri-chiū (Part V.—His Age and Place of Burial)}}.]}}

The Heavenly Sovereign’s august years were sixty-four. His august mausoleum is at Mozu.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXX, Note 1|../Section 130#cite_note-1}}.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXVI.—Emperor Han-zei.}}]}}

His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake dwelt in the palace of Shibakaki at Tajihi,<ref>For Tajihi see {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXII, Note 4|../Section 132#cite_note-4}}. ''Shiba-kaki'' (or ''Shiba-gaki'') signifies “a fence of brushwood.”</ref> and ruled the Empire. The length of this Heavenly Sovereign’s august person was nine feet two inches and a half.<ref>As to the ancient Japanese measures we have no accurate information, and the English equivalents used in this passage correspond but approximately to the modern Japanese standards. The character rendered “line” is {{Japanese|分}}, which denotes the tenth part of a {{Japanese|寸}} or “inch.” Motowori remarks that the dimensions of the teeth are not anything extraordinary judged by the present standard, and supposes that anciently the measures of length must have been smaller than at present.</ref> The length of his august teeth was one inch, and their breadth two lines, and the upper and lower [row] corresponded exactly, like jewels strung {{tooltip|together]|[sic] '[together]'}}. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded the Lady of Tsunu,<ref>''Tsunu no iratsume''. The signification of this name is obscure.</ref> daughter of Kogoto, Grandee of Wani,<ref>''Wani no kogoto no omi''. The meaning of Kogoto is obscure. Wani has already often appeared.</ref> and begot august children: the Lady of Kahi;<ref>''Kahi no iratsume''. Kahi is the name of a province, but it cannot be said for certain that it is from it that this Princess derived her name.</ref> next the Lady of Tsubura<ref>''Tsubura no iratsume''. The meaning of ''Tsubura'' is obscure.</ref> {{sm|(two Deities).}} Again he wedded Oto-hime,<ref>''I.e.'', “the younger princess.”</ref> daughter of the same Grandee, and begot august children: King Takara;<ref>''Takara no miko''. Takara signifies “treasure.”</ref> next the Lady of Takabe,<ref>''Takabe no iratsume''. ''Takabe'' seems to be the name of a place, unless it be considered to be connected with the word ''taka'', “hawk.”</ref>—altogether four Kings [and Queens].<ref>Remember that the single character {{Japanese|王}} includes both sexes.</ref> The Heavenly Sovereign’s august years were sixty. His august mausoleum is on the Moor of Mozu.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXX, Note 1|../Section 130#cite_note-1}}.</ref><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/379 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXXXVII.}}|293}}</noinclude>{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXVII.—Emperor In-giyō<ref>Also pronounced ''In-kiyō''.</ref> (Part I.—Genealogies).}}]}}

His Augustness Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go-no-sukune dwelt in the Palace of Toho-tsu-Asuka,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXIII, Note 13|../Section 133#cite_note-14}}.</ref> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Her Augustness Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime,<ref>This name and the next have already appeared in {{nsl2|Sect. CXVII|../Section 117}}.</ref> younger sister of King Oho-hodo, and begot august children: King Karu of Kinashi;<ref>''Kinashi no Karu no miko''. Karu is properly the name of a place in Yamato which has already often appeared in the text. It is uncertain whether ''kinashi'' is likewise the name of a place or of a particular kind of pear; but Motowori inclines to the former view.</ref> next Nagata-no-oho-iratsume;<ref>''I.e.'', “the great lord of Nagata.” There are many places of this name (lit. “long rice-field”), and it is not known which is here intended.</ref> next King Kuro-hiko of Sakahi;<ref>''I.e.'', “the black prince of Sakahi.” The latter word signifies “frontier.” It is not known where Sakahi is, neither is the reason for the name of “black prince” applied to this personage known (''Conf.'' the “white prince” mentioned a little further on).</ref> next His Augustness Anaho;<ref>Or, “of Anaho,” for Anaho is properly the name of a place in Yamato. Its import is not clear.</ref> next Karu-no-oho-iratsume,<ref>''I.e.'', “the great lady of Karu.”</ref> another name for whom is So-tohoshi-no-iratsume<ref>Written {{Japanese|衣通郎女}}, i.e., “the garment-passing lady.” ''So-tohoshi'' is Motowori’s reading of the characters, the usual rending being ''So-tohori'' (the Intransitive instead of the Transitive form of the Verb). He likewise identifies Koto-fushi (see {{nsl2|Sect. CXVII, Note 9|../Section 117#cite_note-9}}) with this celebrated princess, who is commonly worshipped as Goddess of Poetry. There is much confusion in the traditions concerning her, and Motowori’s notes on the subject in Vol. XXXIV, pp. 53–54 and in Vol. XXXIX of his Commentary, p. 3, should be consulted.</ref> {{sm|(the reason for her being given the august name of Queen So-tohoshi was that the refulgence of her person passed through her garments);}} next King Shiro-biko of Yatsuri;<ref>''Yatsuri no shiro-biko no miko'', ''i.e.'', “the white prince of Yatsuri.” Yatsuri is the name of a place in Yamato. It is written with characters signifying “eight melons.”</ref><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/380 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|294|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />next His Augustness Oho-hatsuse;<ref>''I.e.'', “great Hatsuse,” so called from Hatsuse, a celebrated place in Yamato, which has already been mentioned.</ref> next Tachibana-no-oho-iratsume;<ref>''I.e.'', “the great lady of Tachibana,” the latter being the name of a place in Yamato. The word signifies “orange.”</ref> next Sakami-no-iratsume<ref>''I.e.'', “the lady of Sakami,” the latter being apparently the name of a place either in Harima or in Wohari. Its derivation is not clear.</ref> {{sm|(nine Deities).}} Altogether the Heavenly Sovereign’s august children [numbered] nine Deities {{sm|(five Kings and four Queens)}}. Of these nine Kings and Queens, His Augustness Anaho [was he who {{tooltip|afterwards [ruled|[sic] 'afterwards] ruled'}} the Empire. Next his Augustness Oho-hatsuse ruled the Empire.
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXVIII.—Emperor In-giyō (Part II.—His Sickness is Cured by a Korean Physician).}}]}}

The Heavenly Sovereign, when first about to rule the succession of Heaven’s Sun,<ref>For this expression see {{nsl2|Sect. XXXII, Note 27|../Section 32#cite_note-p103-27}}. The story of the refusal of this monarch to accept the crown which was offered to him by the magnates of the nation is told at considerable length in the parallel passage of the “Chronicles.” According to the same authority he belonged to a collateral branch of the Imperial family, and was therefore not in the regular line of succession.</ref> declined, saying: “I have a long sickness; I cannot rule the sun’s succession.” Nevertheless, as from the Empress downwards all the magnates strongly urged him, he forthwith ruled the Empire. At this time the ruler of Shiragi<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XCVIII, Note 2|../Section 98#cite_note-2}}.</ref> dutifully sent eighty-one vessels with august tribute. Then the chief envoy<ref>Literally, “great messenger.”</ref> sent with the august tribute, whose name was Komu-ha-chimu-kamu-ki-mu,<ref>{{Japanese|金波鎭漢紀武}}. Motowori decides that {{Japanese|金}} is the surname, {{Japanese|波鎭}} an official title, {{Japanese|漢紀}} an official designation of the kinsmen of the Korean King, and {{Japanese|武}} the personal name.</ref> was a man deeply versed in the medical art. So he cured the Heavenly Sovereign’s august sickness.
<section end="s2" />
<section begin="s3" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXXXIX.—Emperor In-giyō (Part III.—He Rectifies the People’s Names).}}]}}

Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, lamenting the transgressions in<section end="s3" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/381 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXL.}}|295}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />the surnames and gentile names of the people of all the surnames and names in the Empire<ref>The original is: {{Japanese|天下氏氏名名人等之氏姓}} which Motowori reads ''ame no shita no uji-uji na-na no hito-domo no uji kabane''.</ref> placed jars [for trial by] hot water<ref>We learn from the “Chronicles” that he whose hand was injured in the process of dipping it into the jar of boiling water was pronounced a deceiver, while those who stood the trial unhurt were considered to be telling the truth.</ref> at the Wondrous Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi,<ref>''Amakashi no koto-ya-so-maga-tsu-hi no saki''. Motowori truly observes that this does not sound like an actual geographical name, but was rather, it may be supposed, a new designation given to Cape Amakashi (see {{nsl2|Sect. LXXII, Note 19|../Section 72#cite_note-19}}) on account of the incident here mentioned. The name reminds us of that one of the deities born from the purification of the person of the creator Izanagi after his return from Hades (see {{nsl2|Sect X, Note 14|../Section 10#cite_note-14).</ref> and deigned to establish the surnames and gentile names of the eighty heads of companies.<ref>''Ya-so tomo-no-wo''. See {{nsl2|Sect. XXXIII, Note 19|../Section 33#cite_note-19}}.</ref> Again the Karu Tribe<ref>''Karu-be''.</ref> was established as the august proxy of King Karu of Ki-nashi; the Osaka Tribe<ref>''Osaka-be'', so called after the Empress’s native place (see {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXVII, Note 3|../Section 137#cite_note-3}}, and {{nsl2|Sect. CXVII, Note 6|../Section 117#cite_note-6}}). The reading of ''Osaka-be'' is given in all the editions to the characters in the text, {{Japanese|刑部}}, where we should expect {{Japanese|忍坂部}}. Motowori’s explanation of the reason why the name was thus written will be found in Vol. XXXIX, p. 19, of his Commentary.</ref> was established as the Empress’s august proxy; and the Kaha Tribe<ref>''Kaha-be''. Motowori supposes that there is here some corruption of the text, as no connection can be discovered between the name of this Tribe and that of the Princess whose proxy the tribe became.</ref> was established as the august proxy of the Empress’s younger sister Ta-wi no Naka-tsu-hime.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXVII, Note 7|../Section 117#cite_note-7}}.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXL.—Emperor In-giyō (Part IV.—His Age and Place of Burial).}}]}}

The Heavenly Sovereign’s august years were seventy-eight. His august mausoleum is at Naga-ye near Wega in Kafuchi.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CIII, Notes 2|../Section 103#cite_note-2}} and {{nsl2|3|../Section 103#cite_note-2}}.</ref><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/382 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|296|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}}}</noinclude>{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLI.—Emperor In-giyō (Part V.—Prince Karu Loves His Sister Princess So-tohoshi).}}]}}

After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign, it was settled that King Karu of Ki-nashi should rule the Sun’s succession.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XXXII, Note 27|../Section 32#cite_note-p103-27}}. The wording of this sentence would make it appear that it was only ''after'' the Emperor In-giyō’s death that King Karu was chosen to succeed him. But probably King Karu had been appointed Heir Apparent ({{Japanese|皇太子}}) during his father’s life-time, as is indeed expressly stated in the “Chronicles,” and is implied in later passages of this work; and what our author meant to say was: “It was settled that King Karu should rule the Empire after the former Sovereign’s decease,” etc.</ref> But in the interval before his accession, he debauched his younger sister the Great Lady of Karu, and sang, saying:
{{bc|“Making rice-fields on the mountain, making hidden conduits run on account of the mountain’s height:—to-day indeed [my] body easily touches the younger sister whom I wooed with a hidden wooing, the spouse for whom I wept with a hidden weeping.”<ref>The meaning of the Song is: “The sister, the mistress, whom I wooed with such difficulty, is now easily mine.”—The first phrase, {{SIC|down|“down}} to mountain’s height,” is but a “Preface” to the poem properly so called, serving to introduce by a ''jeu-de-mots'' the word ''shita-dohi'', which means not only “hidden conduit,” but “hidden wooing.” At the same time the implied comparison of the poet’s secret love of one so difficult to obtain as his own sister, to the course of the water in hidden conduits which is carried up the mountain’s side to irrigate a field perched in a spot almost inaccessible, is by no means devoid of aptness. The word “mountain” ''(yama)'' is in the original preceded by the Pillow-Word ''ashihiki'' (or ''ashibiki) no'', whose signification is obscure and much disputed.</ref>|width=300px}}

This is a Hind-Lifting Song.<ref>''Shirage-uta'' (written phonetically). The interpretation of the term here adopted is that which has the sanction of Motowori and Moribe. They explain it to signify that the voice rose gradually towards the latter part of the Song.</ref> Again he sang, saying:
{{block center/s|width=300px}}“The rattle-rattle of the hail against the bamboo-grass:—After I shall have certainly slept, what though I be plotted against by people! When I shall have<noinclude>{{center block/e}}{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/383 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLII.}}|297}}{{block center/s|width=300px}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />slept a good sleep delightfully, if there is the disorder of the cut ''Hydropyrum latifolium'', let there be disorder,—when I shall have slept a good sleep!”<ref>As in the case of the preceding Song, the first phrase is but a Preface, which plays on the coincidence in sound between the words ''tashi-dashi'', “rattling,” and ''tashika'', “certainly,” i.e. “undisturbedly.” The signification of the Song proper is: “If I shall but have gratified my passion, what care I however men may plot against me? If I can but press my beloved to my bosom, let all things go to rack and ruin, like the ''Hydropyrum latifolium'', a grass which, when cut, falls into disorder!”—Of the sentiment of the Song, the less said the better; but viewed simply from a literary point of view, it is certainly one of the most fascinating little productions of the early Japanese muse, and the literal rendering of it into English does it woful injustice. Moribe rightly rejects Motowori’s proposal to divide the poem in two after the words ''hito hahiyu to mo'', “plotted against by people.” ''Kari-komo no'', “of the ''Hydropyrum latifolium'',” is a Pillow-Word.</ref>{{center block/e}}

This is a Rustic Lifting Song.<ref>''Hinaburi no age-uta''. The commentators have nothing more precise to tell us concerning the expression “Lifting-Song” than that “it refers to the lifting of the voice in singing.”</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLII.—Emperor In-giyō (Part VI.—War Between Prince Karu and Prince Anaho).}}]}}

Therefore all the officials<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXII, Note 4|../Section 112#cite_note-4}}.</ref> and likewise the people of the Empire turned against the Heir Apparent Kara, and towards the August Child Anaho. Then the Heir Apparent Karu, being alarmed, fled into the house of the Grandee the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe,<ref>''Oho-mahe Wo-mahe sukune no omi'' (according to the old reading ''Oho-saki Wo-saki'', etc.). Motowori considers this double name to denote two brothers, the words ''oho'' and ''wo'' (“great” and “small”) naturally lending themselves to the interpretation of “elder” and “younger.” Moribe, on the contrary, thinks that there was but one, and is supported both by the authority of the “Chronicles of Japan” and by the fact that, except in the “Chronicles of Old Matters of Former Ages,” which is believed to be a forgery, no second brother is anywhere mentioned. He explains the use of the double name in the prose text as having crept in through the influence of the text of the following Song (sec {{nsl2|Note 7|#cite_note-7}} below). This seems to the translator the better view.</ref> and made a {{hws|provi|provision}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/384 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|298|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}}}</noinclude>{{hwe|sion|provision}} of implements of war. {{sm|(The arrows made at this time<ref>''I.e.'', “on this occasion.”</ref> were provided with copper arrow-insides;<ref>There is here an evident corruption of the text, and Motowori aptly conjectures that arrow-''heads'', or, as they are called in Japanese, arrow-''points'', are intended. He adds that up till then arrow-heads had always been made of iron.</ref> so those arrows are called by the name of Kara arrows.)}} Prince Anaho likewise made implements of war. {{sm|(The arrows made by this Prince were just the arrows of the present time:<ref>The author’s style is here rather at fault; for he apparently wishes to say that the arrows employed by Prince Anaho were those which had been used in ancient times and were still the most universally employed—that, in fact, they were the usual style of arrow in contradistinction to those of Prince Karu’s invention.</ref> they are called Anaho arrows.)}} Thereupon Anaho raised an army, and beleaguered the house of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe. Then, when be reached the gate, heavy ice-rain<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. LXXXVIII, Note 5|../Section 88#cite_note-5}}.</ref> was falling. So he sang, saying:
{{bc|“Come thus under cover of the metal gate of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe! We will stand till the rain stops.”<ref>The prince, in this Song, bids his troops follow his example, and take refuge from the rain under cover of the gate of Oho-mahe’s house. Such, at least, is the actual sense of the words used; but Motowori sees in them nothing less than a slightly veiled exhortation to his followers to attack the castle, while Moribe, on the other hand, thinks they were meant to convey to Oho-mahe a hint of his presence, and enable the beleaguered prince, for whom (as being his elder brother) Prince Anaho retained a great affection and respect, to devise some method of escape. This seems extremely far-fetched.—The word “metal” probably refers only to the fastenings of the gate, and not to its whole structure.</ref>|width=300px}}

Then the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe came singing, lifting his hands, striking his knees, dancing, and waving his arms. The Song said:
{{bc|“The courtiers are tumultuous, [saying] that the small bell of the garter of the courtiers has fallen off. Country-people, too, beware!”<ref name=p298>The exact purport and application of this Song is disputed, but this much seems clear: that the composer of it seeks to quiet both the besieging army (out of politeness called courtiers), and the peasants who had joined the fray, by making light of the whole occurrence, which he compares to so {{SIC|trival|trivial}} an accident as the falling of a bell from a man’s “garter” or “loggings.” The custom of {{hws|ornament|ornamenting}}</ref>|width=300px}}
{{nop}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/385 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLII.}}|299}}</noinclude><ref follow=p298>{{hwe|ing|ornamenting}} this article of dress with a small bell is, however, not mentioned elsewhere. The word ''yume'', which concludes the Song and is here rendered “beware,” is identified by Motowori and Moribe with the Imperative of the Verb ''imu'', “to avoid,” “to shun,” “not to do.”</ref>This Song is of a Courtier’s Style.<ref>''Miya-hito-buri''. This is one of the cases which lend support to Motowori’s view that the names of the so-called styles of Songs are derived from their initial words.</ref> Singing thus, he came near and said: “August Child of our Heavenly Sovereign! Come not with arms against the King thine elder brother. If thou shouldst come against him with arms, people will surely laugh. I<ref>Written with the humble character {{Japanese|僕}}, “servant.”</ref> will secure him and present him to thee.”<ref>The word used in the text, here and also in the next sentence, is that which properly denotes the presenting of tribute.</ref> Then Prince Anaho disbanded his troops and went away. So the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe secured Prince Karu, and led him forth, and presented him [to Prince Anaho]. The captive Prince sang, saying:
{{bc|“Maiden of heaven-soaring Karu! if thou cry violently, people will know. Cry quietly like the doves on Mount Hasa.”<ref>Another reading gives this sense:
{{bc|“As, if the maiden of heaven-soaring Karu cried violently, people would know, she cries quietly like the doves on Mount Hasa.”|width=250px}}
According to this reading, the poet simply explains the reason of the undemonstrativeness of his mistress’s grief; according to that in the text, he implores her not to weep too passionately.—''Amadamu'' or ''amatobu ya'', “heaven-soaring,” is the Pillow-Word for Karu, applied to it punningly on account of its similarity in sound to the word ''kari'', “a wild-goose,” which well deserves the epithet “heaven-soaring.” Of Mount Hasa nothing is known.</ref>|width=300px}}

Again he sang:
{{bc|“Maiden of heaven-soaring Karu! Come and sleep, and [then] pass on, oh maiden of Karu!”<ref name=p299>Rendered thus according to Moribe’s exegesis, which quite approves itself to the translator’s mind, this Song signifies: “Oh! maiden of Karu! come and sleep with me but once, before my impending banishment renders it hard for</ref>|width=300px}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/386 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|300|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><ref follow=p299>us to meet again.” Motowori chooses to interpret ''nete'' as a crasis of ''nayete'', “bending,” and sees in the Song an invitation to the maiden to come quietly bending her head and passing along quietly so as not to attract observation.—The final word, translated “maiden,” is ''wotome-domo'', properly a Plural, bat here used in a Singular sense, as ''watakushi-domo'', “I” (properly “we”), so constantly is in the modern Colloquial Dialect. For the Pillow-Word “heaven-soaring” see preceding Note.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLIII.—Emperor In-giyō (Part VII.—Death of Prince Karu and Princess So-tohoshi).}}]}}

So Prince Karu was banished to the hot waters of Iyo.<ref>For Iyo see {{nsl2|Sect. V, Note 4|../Section 5#cite_note-p21-4}}. Its hot springs are often mentioned in early documents. Motowori identifies them with a place now called Dō-go ({{Japanese|道後}}).</ref> Again when about to be banished, he sang, saying:
{{bc|“The heaven-soaring birds, too, are indeed messengers. When thou hearest the voice of the crane, ask my name.”<ref>The meaning of this Song is: “I go where perchance no messengers will reach me. But thou must ask tidings of me from the birds.”</ref>|width=300px}}

These three songs are of a Heaven-Soaring style.<ref>''Ama-da-buri''. The title seems to be derived from the initial Pillow-Word of these three Songs.</ref> Again he sang, saying:
{{bc|“If they banish the Great Lord to an island, he will indeed make the remaining return voyage. Beware of my mat! Mat indeed in words,—beware of my spouse!”<ref name=p300>The meaning of this Song seems to the translator to be: “Even if they dare to banish me now, I shall some day return again. Respect my mat during my absence. Mat, indeed! It is my wife that must be respected.” The commentators consider the concluding words to be a command addressed to the wife, and interpret the phrase to mean, “My spouse, beware!” But surely this makes less good sense, and moreover fails to suit the exactly parallel passage in the first Song of {{nsl2|Sect. CXXV|../Section 125}}. By the words “Great Lord” the princely poet denotes himself,—perhaps with a touch of anger at the indignity to which he is subjected. The difficult expression ''funa-amari'' is here, in accordance with Moribe’s view, rendered by the words “remaining voyage,” i.e., “the voyage homeward,” which is that part of a voyage that may be said to remain over for an outward-bound vessel when she has reached her destination. Motowori’s Commentary, Vol.</ref>|width=300px}}
{{nop}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/387 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLIII.}}|301}}</noinclude><ref follow=p300>XXXIX, pp. 50–51, should be consulted for older views of the meaning of the term. The expression “beware of my mat” reminds us that in early days the entire floor of a Japanese room was not matted according to the modern custom, but that each individual had his own mat on which to sit and sleep. Great care was always taken not to defile another’s mat. ''Conf.'' an elegy from the “Collection of a Myriad Leaves” translated by the present writer in his “Classical Poetry of the Japanese,” p. 79.</ref>This Song is of a Partly Lowered Rustic style.<ref>''Hina-buri no kata-oroshi''. Like most of the names of styles of Songs, this one is extremely obscure. The commentators suppose that one part was sung in a lower voice than the rest. But they are merely guessing.</ref> Queen So-tohoshi presented a Song [to him]. That Song said:
{{bc|“Let not thy feet tread on the oyster-shells of the shore of Ahine with its summer herbs! Pass there [after] having made clear!”<ref>The actual words of the Song signify: “Lacerate not thy feet by walking on the unseen oyster-shells of the shore of Ahine that is covered with the summer herbs; but walk there after dawn.” (This is Keichiū’s interpretation of the word ''akashite'', “having made clear,” and is the best in the present writer’s opinion; the later commentators see in it a recommendation to the exiled prince to clear the grass away on either side.) The word ''Ahine'' calls, however, for special explanation in order that the full import of the poem may be brought out. It properly signifies “sleeping together” or “lying on each other,” and is therefore applicable either to the two spouses or to the summer grass. Indeed it is doubtful if it be the name of any real place at all. The word ''natsu-kusa'' may also be taken simply as a Pillow-Word for ''Ahine''.—The total gist of the Song is in any case a warning from the maiden to her lover to guard himself against the perils of the journey.</ref>|width=300px}}

So when afterwards again, being unable to restrain her love, she went after him, she sang, saying:
{{bc|“Thy going has become long past. I will go, oh! to meet thee. Wait! I cannot wait.” {{sm|(What is here called ''yama-tadzu'' is [what is] now [known by the name of] ''tatsuge.)''<ref name=p301>The meaning of this Song is: “It is too long since thy departure. I can wait no longer, but will go and meet thee.”—The Verb “to meet” ''(mukahe)'' is in the original preceded by the Pillow-Word ''yama-tadzu'', which forms the subject</ref>}}|width=300px}}

So when in her pursuit she reached [the place where prince Karu was, he, who had been] pensively waiting, sang, saying:
{{nop}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/388 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|302|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XXXIX.}}}}</noinclude>{{bc|<ref follow=p301>of the note appended to the poem by the compiler. The commentators are not agreed as to the precise nature of the instrument intended; but it seems to have been some kind of axe. The cause of its use as a Pillow-Word for “meeting” is equally disputed. It only occurs written phonetically. The term ''tatsu-ge'', by which it is explained in the text, is there written {{Japanese|造木}}, which does not help us much towards understanding what is meant to be designated.</ref>“Alas! beloved spouse, who settledst the whereabouts of our grave, setting up flags in the great vale, setting up flags in the little vale of Hatsuse the hidden castle! Alas! beloved spouse, whom I see after [our many troubles], prostrate like a ''tsuki'' bow, standing like an ''adzusa'' bow!”<ref>So obscure is this Song in the original, that Motowori confesses himself unable to make any sense of it. The translator has adopted Moribe’s interpretation, according to which the gist of it is this: “Alas! my dear wife, who wast so willing to be for ever united to me that thou didst even fix on the spot in the funereal vale of Hatsuse where we should one day be buried together! Alas for thee, whom at last I now see again!”—In order to arrive at this meaning, Moribe is obliged to prove more or less satisfactorily that the thrice repeated word ''wo'' signifies “vale” or “mountain-fold” the first two times that it occurs, and “grave” the third, and that ''kamoriku no hatsuse'', usually interpreted as secluded “Hatsuse,” means “the hidden castle,” the “final place,” ''i.e.'', “the tomb.” It is also necessary to suppose, without authority, that the flags mentioned by the poet are meant for funeral flags, and that the words “prostrate like a ''tsuki'' bow,” etc., which, according to the laws of Japanese construction, precede instead of following the phrase “alas! beloved spouse,” etc., are but a Preface for the latter.—It will be seen that the foundation on which Moribe’s interpretation rests is slight, and that Motowori was scarcely to be blamed for pronouncing the Song incomprehensible. At the same time the translator has thought it better, by following Moribe, to give ''some'' translation of it than to leave the passage blank. With this warning, the student may search for other possible meanings if he pleases.—Hatsuse is a still existent and celebrated place among the mountains of Yamato. The etymology of the name, unless we accept Moribe’s mentioned above, is obscure. It is now usually pronounced ''Hase''. The ''tsuki'' is said to be almost indistinguishable from the ''keyaki'' tree ''(Zelkowa keaki)''. The ''adzusa'' seems to be the ''Catalpa kaempferi'', but some believe it to be the cherry-tree.</ref>|width=300px}}

Again he sang, saying:
{{block center/s|width=300px}}“Driving sacred piles in the upper reach, driving true piles in the lower reach of the<noinclude>{{center block/e}}{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/389 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XL.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLIII.}}|303}}{{block center/s|width=300px}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />river of secluded Hatsuse, and hanging on the sacrificial piles a mirror, hanging on the true piles true jewels:—if they said that the younger sister whom I love like a true jewel, that the spouse whom I love like a mirror were [there], I would go home, I would long for my country.”<ref>The first half of this Song down to the words “hanging on the true piles true jewels” is a Preface for what follows. The signification of the rest is: “If my dearly loved sister-wife were still at Hatsuse in Yamato, I would fly to her either in thought or deed; but now that she has followed me into exile, the land of exile is good enough.”—Moribe, while allowing the first half of the Song to be a Preface for the rest, contends that it also should be credited with a signification bearing on the subject-matter of the main part of the Song. He supposes, namely, the religious ceremony, whatever it was, of driving piles into the bed or bank of the river and of decorating them with beads and a mirror, to have been one really performed by Princess So-tohoshi to compass her lover’s return. In the translator’s opinion, it is more elegant and more in accordance with Archaic usage to consider the Preface as having no special significance or connection (otherwise than verbal) with the rest of the poem. The word ''i-kuhi'' or ''i-guhi'', rendered “sacred piles,” occasions some difficulty; for it is not certain whether Motowori is right in giving to the initial syllable ''i'' the meaning of “sacred.” It may be simply what has been termed an “Ornamental Prefix,” devoid of meaning. Motowori however points out that this usage of it is restricted to Verbs, and does not occur with Substantives. ''Kamoriku no'', the Pillow-Word for Hatsuse, is rendered by “secluded” in accordance with Mabuchi’s usually accepted derivation from ''komori-kuni'', “retired land.” Moribe, notwithstanding what he has said in his exegesis of the preceding poem ({{nsl2|Note 8|#cite_note-8}}), is willing to allow that, though perhaps not its original, this was its common{{SIC|,}} meaning even in ancient times.</ref>{{center block/e}}

Having thus sung, they forthwith killed themselves together.<ref>''I.e.'', committed suicide together.</ref> So these two songs are Reading Songs.<ref>This expression is interpreted to mean that these Songs were recited in monotone, as one would read a book or tell a tale.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLIV.—Emperor An-kō (Part I.—He Slays King Oho-kusaka).}}]}}

The august child<ref>''I.e.'', Prince. In all other cases we find the word ''mikoto'', “Augustness,” as the title by which the Sovereign is mentioned at the commencement of his reign.</ref> Anaho dwelt at the palace of Anaho at {{hws|Isono|Isonokami}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/390 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|304|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XL.}}}}</noinclude>{{hwe|kami|Isonokami}},<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XLV, Note 16|../Section 45#cite_note-16}}.</ref> and ruled the Empire. The Heavenly Sovereign sent the Grandee of Ne,<ref>''Ne no omi''. The etymology of ''ne'' is obscure.</ref> ancestor of the Grandees of Sakamoto, to the residence of King Oho-kusaka, on behalf of his younger brother Prince Oho-hatsuse to command thus: “I wish Thine Augustness’s younger sister Queen Waka-kusaka to wed Prince Oho-hatsuse. So do thou present her.”<ref>Literally, as “tribute.”</ref> Then King Oho-kusaka did obeisance four times, and said: “Owing to a supposition that there might be some such Great Commands, I have kept her always indoors.<ref>More literally, “I have kept her without putting her out of doors.”</ref> With reverence<ref>''Conf.'' {{nsl2|Sect. IX, Note 4|../Section 9#cite_note-4}} and {{nsl2|Sect. XVIII, Note 14|../Section 18#cite_note-14}}.</ref> will I respectfully offer her according to the Great Commands.” Nevertheless, thinking it disrespectful [merely] to send a message,<ref>Motowori surmises that {{Japanese|其}} may be an error for {{Japanese|者}} in the original of this clause {{Japanese|然言以白事其思旡禮}}.</ref> he forthwith, as a ceremonial gift<ref>{{Japanese|禮物}}. This term corresponds to the modern {{Japanese|結納}}, the name by which the presents which are exchanged at the time of betrothal are designated.</ref> from his younger sister, made [the Grandee of Ne] take a push-wood jewel headdress<ref>The original term ''oshi-ki no tama-kadzura'' is extremely obscure. One of Motowori’s conjectures is that the “push-wood” was a kind of frame by which the jewels or beads, strung on an erect stem of some hard material, were kept firmly attached to the head. Perhaps some notion of the ''coiffure'' intended may be gathered from the plate opposite p. 354 of Part III of vol. VIII of these “Transactions” ([[Author:Josiah Conder (1852-1920)|Mr. J. Conder]]’s paper on “The History of Japanese Costume”).</ref> to present [to the Heavenly Sovereign]. The Grandee of Ne forthwith stole the jewel headdress meant as a ceremonial gift, and slandered King Oho-kusaka, saying: “King Oho-kusaka would not receive the Imperial Commands, but said: ‘An soror mea fiet eædem stirpis [viri] inferior storea?’<ref>''I.e.'', “An soror mea, cujus pater Imperator Nin-toku, fiet uxor præsentis Imperatoris?”—Hujus similitudinis rusticitas et ipsis Japonicis commentatoribus pudori est.</ref> and, grasping the hilt of his cross-sword,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XLV, Note 5|../Section 45#cite_note-5}}.</ref> was angry.” So the Heavenly Sovereign, having in his great anger slain King Oho-kusaka, took that King’s chief wife Nagata-no-oho-iratsume,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXVII, Note 5|../Section 137#cite_note-5}}.</ref> and made her Empress.<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/391 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XL.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLV.}}|305}}</noinclude>{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLV.—Emperor An-kō (Part II.—He is Slain by King Ma-yowa).}}]}}

After this, the Heavenly Sovereign, being on [his] divine couch,<ref>''Conf.'' {{nsl2|Sect. LXIV, Note 2|../Section 64#cite_note-2}}.</ref> was sleeping at midday. Then he spoke to his Empress, saying: “Is there anything on thy mind?”<ref>Literally, “Hast thou anything to think about?” The same construction is used in the next sentence.</ref> She replied, saying: “Being the object of the Heavenly Sovereign’s generous favour, what can there be on my mind?” Hereupon the Empress’s former child,<ref>''I.e.'', her son by her former husband King Oho-kusaka.</ref> King Ma-yowa, who was seven years old that year, happened to be just then playing outside the apartment.<ref>Literally, “below the palace.” The same expression recurs further on. The parallel passage in the “Chronicles” has “below the upper storey,” ''i.e.'', in the court or garden of a two-storeyed house. With the small proportions assumed by Japanese architecture, conversation could well be overheard under these conditions.</ref> Then the Heavenly Sovereign, not knowing that the young King was playing outside the apartment, spoke to the Empress, saying: “I have constantly something upon my mind, namely [the fear] that thy child King Ma-yowa, when he comes to man’s estate, may, on learning that I slew the King his father, requite me with a foul heart.”<ref>''I.e.'', “take vengeance upon me.”</ref> Thereupon King Ma-yowa, who had been playing outside the apartment, and whose ear had caught these words, forthwith watched for the Heavenly Sovereign to be augustly asleep, and, taking the great sword [that lay] by his side,<ref>''Scil.'' by the Emperor’s side.</ref> forthwith struck off the Heavenly Sovereign’s head, and fled into the house of the Grandee Tsubura.<ref>''Tsubura omi''. The etymology of Tsubura is obscure.</ref> The Heavenly Sovereign’s august years were fifty-six. His august mausoleum is on the mound of Fushimi at Sugahara.<ref>For Sugahara see {{nsl2|Sect. LXXV, Note 1|../Section 75#cite_note-1}}. The Fushimi here mentioned, which is in Yamato, must not be confounded with the better known Fushimi in Yamashiro. The popular etymology of this name (and it is to be found in many bonks) traces it to ''fushi-mi'', ''i.e.'', “lying three,” in connection with the story of a man who “lay on the mound for three years.” Probably ''fuse-midzu'', “water laid on,” a name perhaps given on account of an aqueduct or of water-pipes, was the original designation, which has been corrupted.</ref><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/392 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|306|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XL.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLVI.—Emperor An-kō (Part III.—Prince Oho-hatsuse Slays Princes Kuro-biko and Shiro-biko).}}]}}

Then Prince Oho-hatsuse,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXVII, Note 11|../Section 137#cite_note-11}}.</ref> who at that time was a lad, was forthwith grieved and furious on hearing of this event, and went forthwith to his elder brother King Kuro-biko,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXXVII, Note 6|../Section 137#cite_note-6}}.</ref> and said: “They have slain<ref>Literally, “taken.”</ref> the Heavenly Sovereign. What shall be done?” But King Kuro-biko was not startled, and was of unconcerned heart.<ref>''I.e.'', treated the matter with indifference.</ref> Thereupon King Oho-hatsuse reviled his elder brother, saying: “For one thing it being the Heavenly Sovereign, for another thing it being thy brother, how is thy heart without concern?<ref>Literally, “without relying,” as if the speaker meant to say that the dead man could not rely on him for vengeance.</ref> What! not startled, but unconcerned on hearing that they have slain thine elder brother!”—and forthwith he clutched him by the collar, dragged him out, drew his sword, and slew him. Again, going to his elder brother King Shiro-biko, he told him the circumstances as before. The unconcernedness again was like [that shown by] King Kuro-biko. [So King Oho-hatsuse,] having forthwith clutched him by the collar, pulled him along, and dug a pit on reaching Woharida,<ref>In Yamato. The name seems to mean “new tilled field.”</ref> buried him as he stood,<ref>Written {{Japanese|隨立}} in the text followed by Motowori. The other reading {{Japanese|𡓗立}} is untenable.</ref> so that by the time he had been buried up to the loins, both his eyes burst out, and he died.<ref>In order to account for such an effect from so apparently insufficient a cause, Motowori supposes that after the prince had been made to stand up to the height of his loins in the pit, the latter was filled by having stones thrown into it, whereby his feet and legs would be crushed.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLVII.—Emperor An-kō (Part IV.—Death of Prince Ma-yowa and of the Grandee Tsubura).}}]}}

Again he raised an army and beleaguered the house of the Grandee Tsubura. Then [the other side also] raised an army to resist the<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/393 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XL.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLVII.}}|307}}</noinclude>attack,<ref>Literally, “to wait and fight.”</ref> and the arrows that were shot forth were like unto the falling down of the [ears of the] reeds.<ref>The character {{Japanese|來}}, “to come” (here in accordance with English idiom rendered by “down”) is supposed to be an error. One conjectural emendation of it, viz., {{Japanese|盛}}, would suggest the “plentiful” falling of the flowers of the reeds.</ref> Thereupon King Oho-hatsuse, using his spear as a staff, peeped in,<ref>''I.e.'', he lifted himself on tiptoe by leaning on his spear, so as to be able to peep in.</ref> and said: “Is perchance the maiden, with whom I spoke, in this house?”<ref>The maiden thus suddenly introduced into the story is Tsubura’s daughter Kara, whom it must be supposed that the Prince had previously been wooing.</ref> Then the Grandee Tsubura, hearing these commands,<ref>Or rather, “Imperial words.” The application of the characters {{Japanese|詔命}} to the words of one who was not yet actually Emperor is curious.</ref> came forth himself, and having taken off the weapons with which he was girded, did obeisance eight times, and said: “The maiden Princess Kara, whom anon thou deignedst to woo, is at thy service. Again in addition I will present to thee five granaries. {{sm|(What are called the five granaries are now the gardeners of the five villages of Kadzuraki:<ref>''I.e.'', the places where the five granaries originally were are now the five villages inhabited by the men who cultivate the Imperial gardens. For Kadzuraki see {{nsl2|Sect. LV, Note 1|../Section 55#cite_note-1}}.</ref>)}} Meanwhile the reason why she does not come out to meet thee in person is that from of old down to the present time grandees and chiefs have been known to hide in the palaces of Kings, but Kings have not yet been known to hide in the houses of grandees.<ref>Or we may, following Motowori’s proposal, take the character {{Japanese|臣}} in this clause in its slightly different acceptation of “subject,” which better suits the sense. The partly phonetic wording of the next sentence {{Japanese|賤奴意富美者}} shows how the writer was perplexed by the double use of the term.</ref> Therefore I think that, though a vile slave of a grandee<ref>''Q.d.'', in comparison with a prince of the Imperial family, even a grandee was but a vile slave.</ref> exerting his utmost strength in the fight can scarcely conquer, yet must he die rather than desert a Prince who, trusting in him, has entered into his house.”<ref>The character {{Japanese|隨}} in the original of this passage {{Japanese|入坐干隨家}} is corrupt. But the sense remains clear, and it is scarcely worth while looking about for a probable emendation. Motowori has no satisfactory proposal to make.</ref> Having thus spoken, he again took his weapons and<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/394 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|308|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XL.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />went in again to fight. Then, their strength being exhausted and their arrows finished, he said to the Prince: “My<ref>The humble character {{Japanese|僕}}, “servant” is here used for the First Personal Pronoun. The expression {{Japanese|僕者手悉傷}} here literally rendered “my hands are all wounded,” is very curious. Motowori reads it ''ita-te ohinu'', ''i.e.'', “I have received (or suffered from) hurtful hands,” and compares two somewhat similar expressions found in Sect. XLIV (see {{nsl2|Note 33 to that Sect.|../Section 44#cite_note-33}}). The translator may however point out that the similarity is much more apparent in Motowori’s ''kana'' reading than it is in the Chinese text itself. May not the sense of the present passage rather be: “All our men are wounded?” for the word ''te'' ({{Japanese|手}}) “hand,” is frequently used in Japanese,—in compounds at least,— in the sense of “man,” somewhat as it is in English naval, mining, and other technical parlance.</ref> hands are wounded, and our arrows likewise are finished. We cannot now fight. What shall be done?” The Prince replied, saying: “If that be so, there is nothing more to do. [Do thou] now slay me.” So [the Grandee Tsubura] thrust the Prince to death with his sword, and forthwith killed himself by cutting off his own head.
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLVIII.—Emperor An-kō (Part V.—Prince Oho-hatsuse Slays Prince Oshiha).}}]}}

After this Karu-fukuro,<ref>This name has the curious signification of “Korean (or Chinese) hag.”</ref> ancestor of the Dukes of Yama of Sasaki in Afumi,<ref>''Afumi no Sasaki no yama no kimi''. Their legs as they stand are like a moor [covered] with ''wogi'';<ref>The ''Hedysarum esculentum''.</ref> the horns they point up are like withered trees.” At this time [King Oho-hatsuse], taking with him King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, made a progress to Afumi, and on reaching this moor, each of them built a separate temporary palace to lodge in. Then next morning, before the sun had risen, King Oshiha with a tranquil heart rode along on his august horse, and, reaching and standing beside King Oho-hatsuse’s temporary Palace, said to King Oho-hatsuse’s august attendants: “Is he not<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/395 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XL.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CXLIX.}}|309}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />awake yet? He must he told quickly [that I am come]. It is already daylight.<ref>Literally, “the night has already finished dawning.”</ref> He must come to the hunting-ground,”—and forthwith urging his horse, he went forth. Then the people who served the august person of King Oho-hatsuse said: “As [King Oshiha] is a violent-spoken<ref>Motowori endeavours, not very successfully, to explain the use of this epithet by Prince Oho-Hatsuse’s attendants. As the sequel shows, the violence was all on the other side.</ref> Prince, thou shouldst be on thy guard, and likewise it were well to arm thine august person.” Forthwith he put on armour underneath his clothes, took and girded on him his bow and arrows, rode off on horseback, and in a sudden interval setting his horse by the side [of the other King’s], took out an arrow, shot King Oshiha down, forthwith moreover cut his body [to pieces], put [them] into a horse’s manger, and buried them level with the earth.
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CXLIX.—Emperor An-kō (Part VI.—Flight of Princes Ohoke and Woke)}}{{tooltip|].|[sic] '.]'}}}}

Hereupon King Ichi-no-be’s children<ref>Literally “princes” ({{Japanese|王子}}). Their names apparently signify “big basket” and “little basket.”</ref> King Ohoke and King Woke {{sm|(two Deities)}}, having heard of this affray, fled away. So when they reached Karibawi<ref>Known in later times as Kaniha and Kubawi. The name signifies (if the characters with which it is written may be relied on) “the well where the leaves were cut.”</ref> in Yamashiro and were eating their august provisions, an old man with a tattooed face came and seized the provisions. Then the two Kings said: “We do not grudge the provisions. But who art thou?” He replied, saying: “I am a boar-herd in Yamashiro.” So they fled across the River Kusuba,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. LXVI, Note 19|../Section 66#cite_note-19}}.</ref> reached the land of Harima,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. LX, Note 19|../Section 60#cite_note-19}}.</ref> entered the house of a native of that country named Shizhimu,<ref>Or Shizhimi. Properly the name of a village, it is here used as the name of a man. The etymology is obscure.</ref> hid their persons, and worked as grooms and cow-herds.<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/396 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|310|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CL.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part I.—Genealogies).}}]}}

His Augustness Oho-hatsuse-no-waka-take dwelt in the palace of Asakura at Hatsuse,<ref>For Hatsuse see {{nsl2|Sect. CXLIII, Note 8|../Section 143#cite_note-8}}. Several Asakuras are named in the pages of these “Records.” That here named is in Yamato. The name seems to mean “morning store-house.”</ref> and ruled the Empire. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded Queen Wake-kusaka-be, younger sister of King Oho-kusaka {{sm|(no children)}}. Again he wedded Princess Kara, daughter of the Grandee Tsubura, and begot august children: His Augustness Shiraka; next his younger sister Her Augustness Princess Waka-tarashi {{sm|(two Deities)}}.
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLI.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part II.—Various Deeds).}}]}}

So the Shiraka Clan<ref>''Shiraka-be''.</ref> was established as the august proxy of Prince Shiraka. Again the Hatsuse-Clan-Retainers<ref>''Hatsuse-be no toneri''. This Clan was called after the reigning Emperor. Remember that the word “Retainers” is here a “gentile name.”</ref> were established. At this time there came over people from Kure. Again the Kahase Retainers<ref>''Kahase no toneri''. ''Kaha-se'' signifies “river-reach,” and the “Chronicles,” under date of the eleventh year of this reign, tell a story of the appearance of a white cormorant, to commemorate which this family was established. Cormorants, it will be remembered, were used for catching fish in livers: hence the appropriateness of the name bestowed on the family in question.</ref> were established. These people from Kure<ref>The name given by the early Japanese to Wu ({{Chinese|呉}}), an ancient state in Eastern China to the South of the Yang-tzŭ River. In Japanese it however, like other names of portions of China, often denotes the whole of that country in a somewhat vague manner. The derivation of the word ''Kure'' is obscure. The most acceptable proposition is that which would see in it a corruption of the original Chinese term ''Wu'', of which ''Go'' is the Sinico-Japanese pronunciation. But what of the second syllable ''re?''</ref> were lodged<ref>The phrase {{Japanese|安置}} is in this place used for “lodged.”</ref> at Kure-hara. So the place was called by the name of Kure-hara.<ref>''I.e.'', Kure Moor. It is in Yamato. According to the “Chronicles,” the former name of the place had been ''Himokuma-nu''.</ref><section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/397 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CLII.}}|311}}</noinclude>{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLII.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part III.—The Roof of the House of the Great Departmental Lord of Shiki).}}]}}

In the beginning, when the Empress<ref>''I.e.'', ''Waka-kusaka-be''.</ref> dwelt at Kusaka,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XLIV, Note 31|../Section 44#cite_note-31}}. The Kusaka hero mentioned is that in Kafuchi.</ref> [the Heavenly Sovereign] made a progress into Kafuchi by way of the Tadagoye<ref>From ''tada'', “straight” and ''koyuru'' “to cross,” this being a short cut over the mountains.</ref> road at Kusaka. Then, on climbing to the top of the mountain and gazing on the interior of the country, [he perceived that] there was a house built with a raised roof-frame.<ref>The original of this clause is {{Japanese|有上堅魚作舎屋之家}}, which is read ''katsuwo wo agete ya wo tsukureru ihe ari''. The ''katsuwo'' (properly ''katsuwo-gi'' {{Japanese|堅魚木}}) is the name of the uppermost portion of the roof in modern Shintō temples, and apparently in ancient times also in houses that were not devoted to religious purposes. The difficulty is not with the sense, but with the derivation of the word ''katsuwo-gi''. Following the characters with which it is here and elsewhere written, Motowori sees in it a reference to the shape of the blocks of wood resembling “dried bonitoes,” which is the modern signification of ''katsuwo''. But Moribe, in his “Examination of Difficult Words,” proposes a derivation which approves itself more to the present writer’s mind, viz., ''kadzuku wo-gi'' ({{Japanese|戴小木}}), “small timbers atop” (see his “Examination of Difficult Words,” ''s.v.''). Motowori’s Commentary, Vol. XLI, pp. 11–14, should be consulted for a discussion of the whole question of the use of these frames in ancient times, and for the special force to be attributed to the word “raised” ({{Japanese|上}}) in this passage.</ref> The Heavenly Sovereign sent to ask [concerning] that house, saying: “Whose roof with a raised frame is that?” The answer was: “It is the house of the great Departmental Lord of Shiki.”<ref>''Shiki no oho-agata-nushi''. For Shiki see {{nsl2|Sect. LXIII, Note 1|../Section 63#cite_note-1}}.</ref> Then the Heavenly Sovereign said: “What! a slave builds his own house in imitation of the august abode of the Heavenly Sovereign!”—and forthwith he sent men to burn the house [down], when the Great Departmental Lord, with trembling and dread, bowed his head,<ref>''I.e.'', did humble obeisance by prostrating himself on the ground.</ref> saying: “Being a slave, I like a slave did not understand, and have built overmuch. I am in great dread.”<ref>Or, according to the older reading, “This (''i.e.'', thy command) [is to be received with] awe.”</ref> So the thing that he presented as an august offering [in token] of his<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/398 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|312|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />entreaty was a white dog clothed in cloth,<ref>Or, “tied with [a string of] cloth.” The translation follows Motowori’s interpretation.</ref> and with a bell hung [round its neck]; and he made a kinsman of his own, named Koshihaki,<ref>The name signifies “loin-girded,” ''i.e.'', as may he presumed, “wearing a sword.”</ref> lead it by a string and present it [to the Heavenly Sovereign]. So the Heavenly Sovereign ordered them to desist from burning [the house].
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLIII.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part IV.—He Wooes Princess Waka-kusaka-be).}}]}}

Forthwith making a progress to the residence of Queen Waka-kusaka-be, the Heavenly Sovereign sent the dog as a present with a message, saying: “This thing is a strange thing which I got to day on the road. So it is a thing to woo with,”—and so saying, sent it in as a present. Thereupon Queen Waka-kusaka-be sent to say to the Heavenly Sovereign: “It is very alarming that thou shouldst make a progress with thy back to the sun.<ref>For he had come from Yamato in the East to Kafuchi in the West.</ref> So I will come up straight [to the capital], and respectfully serve thee.”<ref>The meaning is: “Thy Majesty must not come to woo me here, as the direction is unlucky. But I will myself come up straightway to the palace to be thine Empress.”</ref> When therefore he returned up and dwelt in the palace, he went and stood on the ascent<ref>The ascent or way up here mentioned is, says Motowori, the Tadagoye Road, and the mountain is Mount Kusaka. See {{nsl2|Sect. CLII, Notes 2|../Section 152#cite_note-2}} and {{nsl2|3|../Section 152#cite_note-2}}.</ref> of that mountain, and sang, saying:
{{block center/s|width=300px}}
“In the hollow between the nearer and the further mountain, this Mount Kusaka-be and Mount Heguri, [is] growing the flourishing broad-leafed bear-oak; at the base grow intertwining bamboos; on the top grow luxuriant bamboos:—we sleep not [now] intertwined like the intertwining bamboos, we sleep not certainly like the<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{center block/e}}{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/399 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CLIV.}}|313}}{{block center/s|width=300px}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" />luxuriant bamboos: [but] oh! my beloved spouse, with whom [I] shall afterwards sleep intertwined!”<ref>In this Song the Emperor consoles himself for the delay in his union with Princess Waka-kusaka-be by reflecting that after all she will soon be his.—The first half of the poem down to the colon and dash is a Preface to the rest. Most of the difficult words occurring in it have been explained in previous notes: for the “broad-leafed bear-oak” see {{nsl2|Sect. LXXII, Note 19|../Section 72#cite_note-19}}; for ''tatami-komo'', the Pillow-Word by which Heguri is preceded in the Japanese text, see {{nsl2|Sect. LXXXIX, Note 12|../Section 89#cite_note-p219-12}}. ''Kusaka-be'' is curious, for whereas it properly signifies Kusaka-Tribe,—this tribe or family being called after the place where they resided,—the place itself came to be renamed after them when the fact of the posterior origin of the family designation had been forgotten. The reason for the mention in the Preface of the oak-tree, which is not referred to in the main text of the poem, is difficult to ascertain. Moribe thinks, however, that it is on account of the luxuriance of its foliage which, as if it were a Preface within the Preface, paves the way for the mention of the thick-growing bamboos. The punning connection between ''tashimi-dake'', “luxuriant bamboos,” and ''tashi ni ha wi-nezu'', “we sleep not certainly,” is necessarily obliterated in the English translation. “Certainly” must be taken in the sense of “undisturbedly.”</ref>{{center block/e}}

And he forthwith sent back a messenger with this Song.<ref>''I.e.'', as may be conjectured, a messenger dispatched to him by his mistress. It seems best to suppose the author to represent the Emperor as not having actually gone to her house at all, but as having only communicated with her by messenger.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLIV.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part V.—Story of the Woman Akawi-ko).}}]}}

Again once when the Heavenly Sovereign, going out for amusement, reached the River Miwa,<ref>''Miwa-gawa''. It is the stream which flows past Hatsuse. For Miwa see {{nsl2|Sect. LXV, Note 8|../Section 65#cite_note-8}}.</ref> there was a girl, whose aspect was very beautiful, washing clothes by the river-side. The Heavenly Sovereign asked the girl, [saying]: “Whose child art thou?” She replied, saying: “My name is Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe.”<ref>''Hiketa-be no Akawi-ko''. ''Hiketa'' is in Yamato. The etymology of the word is obscure. ''Akawi-ko'' signifies “red boar child;” but the appropriateness of the name to the woman in the story is not made to appear.</ref> Then he caused her to be told, saying: “Do not thou marry a<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/400 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|314|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}}}</noinclude>husband. I will send for thee,”—and [with these words] he returned to the palace. So eighty years had already passed while she reverently awaited the Heavenly Sovereign’s commands. Thereupon Akawi-ko thought: “As, while looking for the [Imperial] commands, I have already passed many years, and as my face and form are lean and withered, there is no longer any hope. Nevertheless, if I do not show [the Heavenly Sovereign] how truly I have waited, my disappointment will be unbearable;”—and [so saying] she caused merchandise to be carried on tables holding an hundred,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XXXVII, Note 7|../Section 37#cite_note-7}}.</ref> and came forth and presented [these gifts as] tribute. Thereat the Heavenly Sovereign, who had quite forgotten what he had formerly commanded, asked Akawi-ko, saying: “What old woman art thou, and why art thou come hither?” Then Akawiko replied, saying: “Having in such and such a month of such and such a year received the Heavenly Sovereign’s commands, I have been reverently awaiting the great command until this day, and eighty years have past by. Now my appearance is quite decrepit, and there is no longer any hope. Nevertheless I have come forth in order to show and declare my faithfulness.” Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign was greatly startled [,and exclaimed]: “I had quite forgotten the former circumstance; and thou meanwhile, ever faithfully awaiting my commands, hast vainly let pass by the years of thy prime. This is very pitiful.” In his heart he wished to marry her, but shrank from her extreme age, and could not make the marriage; but he conferred on her an august Song. That Song said:
{{bc|“How awful is the sacred oak-tree, the oak-tree of the august dwelling! Maiden of the oak-plain!”<ref name=p314>Moribe says that, in this Song, the forgetful Monarch calls to mind the majestic and awful appearance of the sacred tree in the temple-grounds, and is moved by this religious thought to repent of his neglectful treatment of her who had so patiently waited for him through so many years. Motowori, on the contrary, sees in the words nothing more than a comparison of the old woman to some sacred tree of immemorial age, and the aversion felt by the monarch to an union with her.—The oak mentioned (the ''Kashi'', ''Quercus myrsinæfolia)'' is an evergreen species. Both Motowori and Moribe consider that ''mimoro'' in the original Japanese of this Song should be taken, not as a proper name (see {{nsl2|Sect. XXVIII,|../Section 28#cite_note-4}}</ref>|width=300px}}
{{nop}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/401 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CLIV.}}|315}}</noinclude><ref follow=p314>{{nsl2|Notes 4|../Section 28#cite_note-4}} and {{nsl2|5|../Section 28#cite_note-5}}), but simply as signifying “a sacred dwelling.” As Miwa is mentioned in the earlier part of the story, it might seem more natural to regard ''mimoro'' as likewise being a Proper Name. But the word ''mimoro'' itself signifying “sacred spot,” the difference between the two views does not amount to much, and it is best to follow native authority. “Oak-plain” ''(kashi-hara)'' means “a place planted with oak-trees.” The first sentence of the Song must be looked on as a sort of Preface to the second.</ref>Again he sang, saying:
{{bc|“The younger chestnut orchard plain of Hiketa:—o si dormivissen cum illâ in juventâ! Oh! how old she has become!”<ref>The first words of this Song down to the colon and dash are a Preface to the Song proper, whose meaning stands in need of no explanation.—Moribe surmises that the word ''kuri'', “chestnut,” was formerly a general name for all sorts of fruits, somewhat like our English word “berry.”</ref>|width=300px}}

Then the tears that Akawi-ko wept quite drenched the red-dyed sleeve that she had on.<ref>The drenching of the sleeve with tears is a common figure in Japanese poetry.</ref> In reply to the great august Song, she sang, saying:
{{bc|“Left over from the piling up of the jewel-wall piled up round the august dwelling,—to whom shall the person of the Deity’s temple go?”<ref name=p315>Or we might (following Moribe) render thus: “Left over from the guarding of the jewel-grove guarded at the august dwelling,” etc. The wording of this Song is far from clear. While Motowori sees in it a reference to the construction of a wall round the grounds of a temple, the overplus of the materials for which sacred wall could not, it may be presumed, be applied to any profane purpose, Moribe disputes the propriety of such an interpretation of the word ''kaki'' which, according to him, denotes the grove planted in temple-grounds, temples never having been surrounded by walls such as Motowori assumes the existence of, nor even by “hedges” or “fences,” which is the more usual acceptation of the term. He thinks, therefore, that the superficial signification of the actual words of the Song is that the priest, who has all his life been in the service of one particular shrine, cannot desert it for the adoration of some other deity. The underlying deeper significance of the little poem is in either case the same: Akawi-ko had, during her long waiting of eighty years, remained true to her first love the</ref>|width=300px}}
{{nop}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/402 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|316|{{asc|“Ko-ji-ki,” or Records of Ancient Matters.}}|[{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}}}</noinclude><section begin="s1" /><ref follow=p315>Emperor. For every reason it had been impossible for her ever to give her affections to another, and she had now come up to the capital to demonstrate to him who had forgotten her the unchangeable nature of her feelings.</ref>Again she sang, saying:
{{bc|“Oh! how enviable is she who is in her bloom like the flowering lotus,—the lotus of the inlet, of the inlet of Kusaka.”<ref>This pretty little poem is too clear to need any comment. Moribe supposes that some lotuses brought from Kusaka may have been among the presents made by Akawi-ko to the Emperor. In the original Japanese the reference to the lotuses comes first, as a sort of preface to the rest of the poem. The laws of English construction necessitate its being put last in the translation.</ref>|width=300px}}

Then the old woman was sent back plentifully endowed. So these four Songs are Quiet Songs.<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXXIV, Note 19|../Section 124#cite_note-19}}.</ref>
<section end="s1" />
<section begin="s2" />{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLV.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part VI.—He Makes a Progress to Yeshinu).}}]}}

When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the palace of Yeshinu,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. XLVI, Note 3|../Section 46#cite_note-3}}.</ref> there was on the bank of the Yeshinu river a girl of beautiful appearance. So having wedded this girl, he returned to the Palace. Afterwards, when he again made a progress to Yeshinu, he halted where he had met the girl, and in that place raised a great august throne,<ref>See {{nsl2|Sect. CXII, Note 2|../Section 112#cite_note-2}}.</ref> seated himself on that august throne'';'' played on his august lute, and made the maiden dance. Then he composed an august Song on account of the maiden’s good dancing. That Song said:
{{bc|“Oh! that the maiden dancing to the lute-playing of the august hand of the Deity seated on the throne might continue for ever!”<ref>This Song presents no difficulties. In it the Emperor speaks of himself as a Deity, and is enthusiastically praised by the commentator Moribe for so doing.</ref>|width=300px}}<section end="s2" /><noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>

==== PAGE Page:Kojiki by Chamberlain.djvu/403 ====
<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="TE(æ)A,ea." />{{rh|{{asc|Vol. XLI.}}]|{{asc|Vol. III. Sect. CLVI.}}|317}}</noinclude>{{c|[{{asc|Sect. CLVI.—Emperor Yū-riyaku (Part VII.—The Horse-fly and the Dragon-fly).}}]}}

When forthwith he made a progress to the Moor of Akidzu,<ref>''Akidzu-nu''. See {{nsl2|Note 4|#cite_note-4}} to this Section.</ref> and augustly hunted, the Heavenly Sovereign sat on an august throne. Then a horse-fly bit his august arm, and forthwith a dragon-fly came and ate up<ref>Or, “bit.”</ref> the horse-fly, and flew [away]. Thereupon he composed an august Song. That Song said:
{{bc|“Who is it tells in the great presence that game is lying on the peak of Womuro at Mi-yeshinu? Our Great Lord, who tranquilly carries on the government, being seated on the throne to await the game, a horse-fly alights on and stings the fleshy part of his arm fully clad in a sleeve of white stuff, and a dragon-fly quickly eats up that horse-fly. That it might properly bear its name, the laud of Yamato was called the Island of the Dragon-Fly.”<ref name=p317>The signification of the greater portion of this Song is clear enough, and is sufficiently explained by the context. The word “who” however admits of two interpretations, Motowori taking it to signify “some one,” whereas Moribe, keeping the literal meaning of “who?”, sees in it an angry exclamation of the monarch’s at having been brought out to the hunt under exaggerated promises of game. ''Womuro'' means “little cave,” but is here a proper name. ''Mi-yeshinu'' is a form of the word Yoshino which is frequently met with in poetry, the syllable ''mi'' being probably, as Mabuchi tells us in his “Commentary on the Collection of a Myriad Leaves,” equivalent to ''ma'', and therefore simply an “Ornamental Prefix.” The phrase “tranquilly carries on the government” represents the Japanese ''yasumi-shishi'', the Pillow-Word for ''wa ga oho-kimi'', “our Great Lord,” which latter phrase descriptive of the Sovereign is here put into the Sovereign’s own month. “Of white stuff,” ''shiro-tahe no'', is another Pillow-Word. The only real difficulty in this Song meets us in the interpretation of its concluding sentence. The meaning apparently intended to be conveyed is that it was in order to prove itself worthy of its name that the dragon-fly performed the loyal deed which forms the subject of the tale. But if so, the author forgets that it was not the dragon-fly that was</ref>|width=300px}}
{{nop}}<noinclude>{{rule}}{{smallrefs}}</noinclude>
